g.text: LLM agents deployed for CLI tasks
Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed for
command-line interface (CLI) tasks, from software engineering to
system administration (Yang et al., 2024a; Jimenez et al., 2023).
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=2) Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed for command-line interface (CLI) tasks, from software engineering to system administration (Yang et al., 2024a; Jimenez et al., 2023).

g.text: These agents interact with terminal environments through iterative reasoning
and action cycles (Yao et al., 2022), executing commands and processing
g.title: N2 [Context] (cites=1) These agents interact with terminal environments through iterative reasoning and action cycles (Yao et al., 2022), executing commands and processing outputs to accomplish complex goals.

g.text: Recent benchmarks such as Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al., 2026) evaluate
agents on realistic CLI tasks requiring multi-step reasoning, revealing that
long-horizon interactions pose significant challenges: as trajectories grow,
g.title: N3 [Context] (cites=1) Recent benchmarks such as Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al., 2026) evaluate agents on realistic CLI tasks requiring multi-step reasoning, revealing that long-horizon interactions pose significant challenges: as trajectories grow, context windows fill with observation histories, leading to timeout failures and degraded performance.

g.text: Existing agent frameworks address context growth through LLM-based
summarization, compressing older observations into free-form summaries (Wang
g.title: N4 [Prior_Work] (cites=1) Existing agent frameworks address context growth through LLM-based summarization, compressing older observations into free-form summaries (Wang et al., 2025).

g.text: However, CLI environments present unique challenges for such
g.title: N5 [Limitation] (cites=0) However, CLI environments present unique challenges for such approaches.

g.text: free-form summaries lose exact CLI tokens
Terminal outputs contain exact tokens critical for task completion—specific
error messages, file paths, and command flags—that free-form summaries may
g.title: N6 [Limitation] (cites=0) Terminal outputs contain exact tokens critical for task completion—specific error messages, file paths, and command flags—that free-form summaries may omit or paraphrase incorrectly.

g.text: Additionally, agents may enter unproductive loops, repeatedly
executing the same failing command without making progress.
g.title: N7 [Context] (cites=0) Additionally, agents may enter unproductive loops, repeatedly executing the same failing command without making progress.

g.text: stuck detectors terminate but don't recover
Current stuck detectors typically terminate execution upon
detecting such patterns, preventing resource waste but not helping
g.title: N8 [Limitation] (cites=0) Current stuck detectors typically terminate execution upon detecting such patterns, preventing resource waste but not helping the agent recover.

g.text: We present LASCon (Loop-Aware Scratchpad Condensation), a training-free
scaffold intervention that addresses these challenges through two
g.title: N9 [Method] (cites=0) We present LASCon (Loop-Aware Scratchpad Condensation), a training-free scaffold intervention that addresses these challenges through two complementary modules.

g.text: DCC: rule-based CLI extraction, logs to disk
The Deterministic CLI Condenser (DCC) replaces LLM-based
summarization with rule-based extraction tailored to CLI outputs,
preserving commands, exit codes, error lines, and truncated
outputs while offloading full logs to disk.
g.title: N10 [Method] (cites=0) The Deterministic CLI Condenser (DCC) replaces LLM-based summarization with rule-based extraction tailored to CLI outputs, preserving commands, exit codes, error lines, and truncated outputs while offloading full logs to disk.

g.text: The Progress-Conditioned Loop Controller (PLC) converts loop
detection into action-space shaping, blocking specific repeated
actions to force exploration of alternatives rather than
g.title: N11 [Method] (cites=0) The Progress-Conditioned Loop Controller (PLC) converts loop detection into action-space shaping, blocking specific repeated actions to force exploration of alternatives rather than terminating execution.

g.text: On Terminal-Bench 2.0 with Qwen3-32B, LASCon achieves 68.8% completion rate
(+21.2pp over baseline) while eliminating all timeout failures.
g.title: N12 [Result] (cites=0) On Terminal-Bench 2.0 with Qwen3-32B, LASCon achieves 68.8% completion rate (+21.2pp over baseline) while eliminating all timeout failures.

g.text: LASCon: A training-free scaffold combining deterministic CLI
condensation with progress-conditioned loop control, deployable
with any LLM backend without fine-tuning.
g.title: N13 [Contribution] (cites=0) LASCon: A training-free scaffold combining deterministic CLI condensation with progress-conditioned loop control, deployable with any LLM backend without fine-tuning.

g.text: Empirical finding: Structured context management through DCC alone
deterministic condensation outperforms LLM summarization for CLI
g.title: N14 [Contribution: Empirical finding] (cites=0) Empirical finding: Structured context management through DCC alone achieves 70.0% completion (+18.8pp), demonstrating that deterministic condensation outperforms LLM summarization for CLI contexts.

g.text: PLC is safety net, not primary driver
Analysis: Loop-induced failures are rare (2.5% in baseline) and
eliminated by prompting alone; PLC serves as a conservative safety
net (0.12% block rate) rather than a primary improvement
g.title: N15 [Contribution: Analysis] (cites=0) Analysis: Loop-induced failures are rare (2.5% in baseline) and eliminated by prompting alone; PLC serves as a conservative safety net (0.12% block rate) rather than a primary improvement mechanism.
